name: B7-33
lead: B7-33 is a laboratory-designed, single-chain peptide derived from the B-chain of human relaxin-2, a pleiotropic hormone with vasodilatory and anti-fibrotic properties. It was engineered as a simpler and cheaper mimic of recombinant relaxin-2 (serelaxin), which is costly and laborious to produce [1][2].

B7-33 acts on the relaxin receptor RXFP1 but is described as a functionally selective agonist: it engages some of the receptor's signalling pathways (notably ERK1/2 phosphorylation) while only weakly stimulating others such as cAMP [1][4]. Published work on it consists of cell, mouse and rat studies of vascular function, cardiac remodelling and fibrosis [2][4][5]. It is not an approved medicine, and no human clinical trial has been published.

It appears in peptide-vendor catalogues in the recovery and tissue-repair category, but the sources reviewed contain no material on how looksmaxxing communities discuss it, and its link to appearance is through tissue repair (scarring and fibrosis are among the processes studied).

paras: Human relaxin-2 signals through RXFP1, a G protein-coupled receptor, activating several pathways including cAMP and MAP-kinase signalling [1]. A 2016 chemical-biology study reported that B7-33, a single-chain peptide based on the relaxin B-chain, is a functionally selective RXFP1 agonist that preferentially activates ERK1/2 phosphorylation over cAMP accumulation [1]. Later work on myocardial infarction in mice described the same pathway bias [4].

Medicinal-chemistry papers have continued to modify the peptide, for example with lipidation to improve stability in serum without altering activity, and in the search for a minimal potent relaxin-2 derivative [8][10]. A review covers single-chain peptide agonists of the relaxin receptors more broadly [6].

No studies found in humans. Published research is preclinical: a rodent study reported that B7-33 reproduced vasoprotective effects of serelaxin [2]; a mouse myocardial-infarction study reported attenuated adverse cardiac remodelling [4]; a rat cardiomyopathy model reported more rapid reduction of left-ventricular fibrosis than the ACE inhibitor perindopril [5]; a mouse study examined central relaxin-receptor activation and inflammatory pain [9]; and implant coatings releasing B7-33 were reported to reduce fibrotic encapsulation [7]. A renal-fibrosis imaging method has also been used to assess B7-33 and other anti-fibrotic agents [3].

B7-33 is described in research literature rather than in clinical practice, and has no approved indication. The sources reviewed contain no documented community discussion of its use for appearance purposes.

timeline.event: B7-33 reported as a functionally selective RXFP1 agonist [1].
Reported to replicate vasoprotective effects of serelaxin in vascular studies [2].

card.summary: A lab-made relaxin mimic studied in animals for fibrosis; no human trials and no documented appearance use.
card.note: Preclinical only; no human safety or efficacy data.

quick.overview:
B7-33 is a short peptide designed to imitate part of the hormone relaxin-2, which has anti-fibrotic and blood-vessel-relaxing effects. It was built because the natural hormone is expensive to make.

All published findings are from cells, mice and rats, mainly on heart and kidney fibrosis. No human trial exists, and no source reviewed describes appearance-related use.
quick.mechanism: It binds the relaxin receptor RXFP1 but is biased, activating ERK1/2 signalling more than cAMP, according to the research that characterised it.
quick.risks: Human safety is unstudied. It is not an approved drug anywhere; availability is limited to research-chemical channels.
